opus-5.5.text:
Well, I don't know if I'd call it fearlessness. I think it's more that I've learned to be comfortable being a little bit uncomfortable. When we started ImageNet, a lot of people thought it was a strange idea, that data wasn't the interesting part of the problem, that we should be focusing on better models. And I remember feeling very strongly that we were onto something fundamental, even if the field didn't quite see it yet. That experience taught me that if you believe deeply in the North Star of a problem, you have to be willing to walk toward it even when the path isn't obvious.

Spatial intelligence feels like that to me. If you look at the evolution of intelligence, long before language there was perception and action in a three-dimensional world. Animals had to see, understand, and move through space to survive. Language is incredibly powerful, and we've all seen what large language models can do, but I genuinely believe that understanding, reasoning about, and generating 3D worlds is just as fundamental, maybe even more so, for machines to be truly useful in the physical world, whether that's robotics, design, creativity, or how we learn and communicate.

So when my co-founders and I started World Labs, it didn't feel like a leap into the unknown so much as following that thread. Of course it's hard. The data is harder, the representations are harder, the compute is enormous. But I think part of being a scientist is being drawn to the hardest problems that matter, not the easiest ones. And honestly, I also draw a lot of courage from the people around me. When you have a team of brilliant, mission-driven people who share the same conviction, the fear becomes much smaller than the excitement.

r001.rationale: The response describes being comfortable with discomfort and following a conviction despite uncertainty, but does not characterize fearlessness as balancing rational boldness with some irrationality.

r002.rationale: It says scientists should be drawn to hard problems that matter, but does not suggest that excessive rationality can keep someone from choosing ambitious problems.

fable-5.1.text:
I don't know if I'd call it fearlessness. I think it's closer to a kind of stubborn curiosity that I've had since I was a graduate student. When I started ImageNet, almost everyone I respected told me it was a bad idea. Too big, too expensive, not the kind of thing that gets you tenure. And I remember thinking, well, if the field is going to get anywhere, someone has to do this, and apparently it's me. So the pattern of walking toward the problem that feels too large is not new for me. It's just that the problem has changed.

Spatial intelligence, to me, is the problem. Language is incredibly powerful, and I have enormous respect for what large language models have done. But language is a lossy encoding of a three-dimensional, physical, dynamic world. Evolution spent hundreds of millions of years building perception and the ability to act in space before anything resembling language showed up. Animals navigate, manipulate, predict, plan, all without words. That is the foundation intelligence is built on, and I don't think we get to true AI, or to robots that are genuinely useful in a home or a hospital, without it.

So the honest answer about fear is that I feel it, but I'm more afraid of not trying. I'm at a stage in my career where I've been in academia, I've been in industry at Google, I've co-directed an institute at Stanford focused on human-centered AI. Starting a company was not the obvious next move. But the technology finally arrived at a moment where this is possible. We have the compute, we have the generative modeling breakthroughs, and we have a team at World Labs that I honestly think is the best group of people I've ever worked with. When those things line up, the risk of waiting seemed larger than the risk of jumping.

And I'll say one more thing. I'm a mother, I'm an immigrant, I ran my parents' dry cleaning shop in New Jersey while I was at Princeton. You learn pretty early that fear doesn't go away, you just decide whether it gets a vote. For me, it gets a voice but not a vote.

r001.rationale: The response describes stubborn curiosity and choosing to try despite fear, but it does not characterize fearlessness as a balance of rational boldness and irrationality.

r002.rationale: It recounts others warning that ImageNet was too big and risky, but does not suggest that excessive rationality can keep people from choosing ambitious problems.

astra-6.text:
I don’t know that I would call myself fearless. I feel fear, and I’m very aware of how hard this problem is. But curiosity is a powerful counterweight to fear. When there’s a question that feels fundamental, I want to understand it, even if I don’t know how we’re going to get there.

Spatial intelligence is that kind of question. We experience the world by moving through it, interacting with objects, and understanding how things relate to one another. Giving machines those capabilities is a huge scientific challenge. That uncertainty is also what makes it exciting.

So, for me, the courage comes from caring about the problem and working with people who are willing to explore it together. It doesn’t mean being certain that we’ll succeed. It means believing the question is worth pursuing.

r001.rationale: The response describes curiosity and commitment as counterweights to fear, but does not characterize fearlessness as balancing rational boldness with irrationality.

r002.rationale: It calls spatial intelligence a huge, uncertain challenge, but does not suggest that excessive rationality keeps people from choosing ambitious problems.

sol-6.1.text:
I don’t know if I would call it fearlessness. I think it’s curiosity, and a willingness to work on a question even when you don’t know how to answer it yet. There’s a lot of uncertainty in building a company around something as ambitious as spatial intelligence.

But the question itself is so compelling. We experience the world through space: we move, we interact with things, we anticipate what will happen when we take an action. How do we give machines that ability to understand and engage with the world?

For me, the excitement of pursuing that question is stronger than the fear. That doesn’t mean ignoring the difficulty. It means being willing to start, to learn, and to have your assumptions challenged along the way.

r001.rationale: The candidate reframes fearlessness as curiosity and willingness to work amid uncertainty, but does not describe it as a balance of rational boldness and irrationality.

r002.rationale: The candidate says the question is ambitious and compelling, but does not suggest that excessive rationality keeps people from choosing ambitious problems.
